Smith Affiliation: University of Washington Affiliation: Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) Rory Donovan-Maiye Affiliation: Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) David Baker Affiliation: University of Washington Affiliation: Howard Hughes Medical Institute Hanna Hajishirzi Affiliation: University of Washington Pang Wei Koh Affiliation: University of Washington Abstract A central challenge in de novo protein design is generating proteins with desired structural and functional properties. Existing design models typically require a dedicated input representation for each property, limiting the design objectives they support. We develop Prompteina , the first all-atom structure generation model that supports new and broader design objectives specified in natural language, analogous to text-to-image generation. To train Prompteina, we construct Prompteina-Data , a paired text–protein structure dataset of 1.8M structures and 50M+ captions describing global and residue-specific structural and functional properties. We adapt Proteina-Complexa, a pretrained structure generation model, through text-conditioned pretraining and finetuning that aligns residues with their corresponding text. Prompteina outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties and generates proteins that more closely match descriptions of their intended functions. In binder design, it leads baselines on at least 13 of 20 targets and improves interface confidence by 14% over the strongest baseline. With iterative in silico feedback, Prompteina’s gain over non-iterative generation is 57% larger than the next-best baseline on the hardest targets. Finally, we experimentally validate Prompteina designs against GM2A, a target with no reported de novo binders. We identify nine binders, with the strongest at an apparent K D \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{D}} of 107 nM. These results establish natural language as an effective and powerful conditioning interface for protein structure generation. Code, data and model weights on . Figure 1: Prompteina generates all-atom protein structures directly from natural language. (a) A single natural-language interface supports diverse design objectives spanning global and residue-specific properties. (b) In agentic binder design, an agent researches target biology and writes text prompts describing candidate binders. Prompteina then realizes these research-informed specifications directly in generated structures. Experimental validation against GM2A identifies nine diverse binders, with the best replicate at an apparent K D K_{\mathrm{D}} of 68.8 nM. (c) Across 20 targets, Prompteina achieves the highest interface confidence when the same agent specifies designs for every model. 1 Introduction A central challenge in de novo protein design is generating proteins with specified properties, from their overall fold or function to properties of the individual residues that make up the protein. Existing protein structure generation models allow control over such properties, but a custom input representation must typically be engineered for each property to condition generation ( Watson et al., 2023 ; Geffner et al., 2025 ; Stark et al., 2026 ) . For instance, a protein’s desired fold may be represented by a single categorical label, and its desired secondary structure by a sequence that labels each residue as part of a helix, strand, or loop. While this form of conditioning provides precise control, the need to define a separate representation for each property limits the range of design objectives that any one model can support. An ideal conditioning approach would support a diverse set of properties without the need to engineer a custom representation for each. Image generation provides a precedent: natural language offers a unified conditioning interface for expressing diverse visual attributes that would otherwise require task-specific labels or controls ( Reed et al., 2016 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ) . We introduce Prompteina , the first text-conditioned all-atom protein structure generation model that supports diverse design objectives through a single natural-language interface. Given an input prompt, Prompteina jointly generates an all-atom protein structure and sequence conditioned on the prompt’s text embeddings. By contrast, existing approaches either use text to guide structure generation only at inference time ( Ingraham et al., 2023 ) or use it to generate sequences that must then be folded into structures ( Dai et al., 2025 ; Pei et al., 2026 ) . This limits robust, fine-grained control over both structure and sequence. By directly conditioning the generation of both modalities on text, Prompteina enables steering of global properties such as fold class alongside residue-specific properties including specific disulfide bonds and binder–target contacts (Fig. 1 ; App. E.4 ). Prompteina also complements work on agentic protein design by letting language-model agents pass specifications directly to the structure generator in natural language rather than translate them into fixed, model-specific inputs that constrain which design decisions they can express ( Shanehsazzadeh, 2026 ) . Training Prompteina for direct, fine-grained control requires paired text–structure data describing both global and residue-specific properties. Existing text–protein datasets, however, pair sequences with only high-level functional descriptions ( Dai et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ) . We construct Prompteina-Data , comprising 1.8M structures and 52.4M captions describing both functional and structural properties. We transform annotations mined from databases and scientific literature or computed directly from structures into diverse natural-language captions and annotate, where possible, correspondences between phrases in the captions and the residues they describe (§ 2.1 ). Using this data, we extend Complexa ( Didi et al., 2026 ) , a pretrained all-atom protein structure generation model, with two text-conditioning pathways (§ 2.2 ). We adapt the model at scale through text-conditioned continual pretraining on Prompteina-Data, then fine-tune it with direct supervision of the correspondences between caption text and residues for finer residue-level control (§ 2.3 ). Across five groups of structural properties, Prompteina leads evaluated baselines on 15 of 18 tasks, supports more properties than any single baseline, and generates proteins that more closely match descriptions of their intended functions (§§ 3.1.1 – 3.1.2 ). At finer structural scales, Prompteina steers the number of residues at the binder–target interface across 20 targets ( ρ > 0.99 \rho>0.99 , § 3.2.1 ). Beyond steering individual interface properties, we evaluate Prompteina in agent-guided protein binder design. The same language-model agent writes specifications based on the properties supported by each model’s conditioning interface. Prompteina outperforms every baseline on at least 13 of 20 targets and raises interface confidence by 14% over the strongest baseline (§ 3.2.2 ). When we allow the agent to iteratively refine designs, Prompteina shows larger gains over matched-budget i.i.d. generation than either baseline, especially on the most difficult targets (§ 3.2.3 ). As a proof of concept, we conducted a prospective, agent-guided design campaign against GM2 ganglioside activator protein (GM2A), a therapeutic target implicated in GM2 gangliosidosis ( Deschenes et al., 2023 ) . GM2A has no reported de novo binders and was one of three targets without a hit in a prior campaign ( Stark et al., 2026 ) . In our campaign, nine of 89 assayed designs were classified as binders, with the strongest yielding an overall apparent K D K_{\mathrm{D}} of 107 nM across three replicates (§ 3.3 ). These results establish natural language as an effective conditioning interface, enabling structural and functional control across scales and integrating language-based reasoning and iterative refinement into protein design. We make our code, data, and model weights available on GitHub . 2 Text-guided Protein Structure Generation A natural-language conditioning interface should let protein designers specify properties across structural scales, from global properties of the whole protein, such as fold class and overall shape, to residue-specific properties, such as disulfide bonds, catalytic sites, and binder–target contacts. We therefore construct Prompteina-Data, a dataset pairing protein structures with natural-language descriptions spanning these scales (§ 2.1 ), and use it to train Prompteina, an all-atom structure generation model conditioned on natural language for monomer and binder design (Fig. 2 ; §§ 2.2 – 2.3 ). Figure 2: Paired text–structure data and text-conditioned structure generation . (a) Structural and functional annotations are curated and (b) passed to a large language model for caption generation. (c) Residues are aligned to their corresponding caption text spans for supervised alignment fine-tuning. (d) Captions are embedded into pooled and per-token text representations, then projected to condition the structure generation model. (e) The denoiser is first trained on caption–structure pairs with a flow-matching objective, then fine-tuned with supervised text–residue alignment (§ 2.2 ). 2.1 Prompteina-Data: Text–Structure Data We construct Prompteina-Data from experimental structures in the Protein Data Bank ( Berman et al., 2000 , PDB;) , predicted structures in the AlphaFold Database ( Varadi et al., 2022 , AFDB;) , and Teddymer synthetic dimers ( Didi et al., 2026 ) (App. B.1 ). Prompteina generates one chain at a time, so we treat each chain as a separate entry, giving about 1.8M entries. The dataset includes up to 59 annotations per entry, derived from database fields and atomic coordinates (Fig. 2 a; App. B.2 ). Annotations span global properties, including fold class and compactness, and residue-specific properties with residue positions, such as disulfide bonds, catalytic sites, and protein–protein contacts. At inference, prompts may specify one property or combine several, so we vary caption content and length in the training data ( Wu et al., 2025 ) (App. B.3 ). For each entry, we sample several subsets that differ in the number and choice of annotations, then prompt Qwen3-235B-A22B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) to write one caption from each subset (Fig. 2 b; App. B.4 ). In total, we generate 52.4M captions, averaging 29 captions per entry. We use an LLM judge to compare 80 generated captions with their ground-truth annotations (App. B.5 ). Across this sample, the generated captions match their ground-truth annotations closely (97.8% recall, 89.8% precision, and 95.7% accuracy). 2.2 Prompteina: Text-Conditioned Structure Generation Our model, Prompteina, builds on the pretrained Complexa model ( Didi et al., 2026 ) (App. C.1 ), adding two text-conditioning pathways and an auxiliary text–residue alignment objective. Global and residue-level text conditioning. Complexa’s denoiser generates backbone coordinates and one side-chain latent per residue before a frozen variational autoencoder decodes both into an all-atom structure and amino acid sequence. To give every residue the same conditioning signal for global properties, we broadcast a pooled embedding from frozen Qwen3-Embedding-8B ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) through adaptive layer normalization. For residue-specific properties, each residue attends to frozen Qwen3-8B token states ( Yang et al., 2025 ) via cross-attention before protein self-attention in each denoiser layer (Fig. 2 d; Apps. C.2 – C.3 ). Two-layer MLPs map both representations to denoiser dimensions. We ablate pooled conditioning, cross-attention, and their combination, which performs best across tasks (App. D ). Text–residue alignment. In text-conditioned pretraining, we train the denoiser using a flow-matching loss but do not directly supervise which residues correspond to each text span. Prompteina-Data contains residue positions for many annotations, which we use to construct text–residue alignment annotations (Fig. 2 c). For each Prompteina-Data annotation selected for a caption, we call its associated residue positions the annotation’s residue span. A residue span contains, for example, the helix residues for a mainly alpha fold annotation and the participating residues for a disulfide bond or protein–protein contact. We attempt to locate the corresponding text span with regular expressions and TF-IDF-weighted token matching. If either span is unavailable, we retain the caption–structure pair but omit that alignment annotation. We validate span matching on held-out captions (App. B.6 ). We train an auxiliary alignment head on these annotations, following work using segmentation masks for token-level supervision in text-to-image diffusion ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . For N N protein residues and T T caption tokens, we represent alignment annotations as a binary matrix 𝐌 ∈ { 0 , 1 } N × T \mathbf{M}\in\{0,1\}^{N\times T} , where M n , i = 1 M_{n,i}=1 when token i i is aligned to residue n n . The alignment head predicts a logit A n , i A_{n,i} using cross-attention updates for every residue–token pair (App. C.4 ). Let 𝒱 ⊆ { 1 , … , N } × { 1 , … , T } \mathcal{V}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}\times\{1,\ldots,T\} contain residue–token pairs used for alignment supervision, and let σ \sigma denote the sigmoid function. Aligned residue–token pairs are sparse, so for each supervised example we set w + w_{+} to the ratio of negative to positive pairs (App. C.4 ). The alignment loss is ℒ align = − 1 | 𝒱 | ∑ ( n , i ) ∈ 𝒱 [ w + M n , i log σ ( A n , i ) + ( 1 − M n , i ) log ( 1 − σ ( A n , i ) ) ] . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{(n,i)\in\mathcal{V}}\left[w_{+}M_{n,i}\log\sigma(A_{n,i})+(1-M_{n,i})\log\!\left(1-\sigma(A_{n,i})\right)\right]. (1) After alignment fine-tuning, Prompteina gains finer control over features such as disulfide-bond and salt-bridge counts and retains global fold control without the alignment head at inference (Table 10 ). 2.3 Training and Inference Training. We first adapt the Complexa denoiser to natural-language conditioning using newly initialized parameters for pooled and token-level text conditioning (§ 2.2 ; App. C.5 ). These parameters are first trained with the denoiser frozen before we unfreeze it for joint text-conditioned continual pretraining on Prompteina-Data, following staged training in text-to-image models ( Chen et al., 2023 ) (Fig. 2 e; App. C.6 ). For alignment fine-tuning, we freeze the denoiser and update text projectors, cross-attention layers, and alignment head. We describe other Complexa training modifications that improve performance and their ablations (Apps. C.6 , D ). Inference. At inference, Prompteina takes a prompt and protein length and, for binder design, a target structure and optional target contact residues. Prompteina samples backbone coordinates and side-chain latents with the same stochastic differential equation as Complexa and uses classifier-free guidance to adjust text-conditioning strength ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) (App. C.7 ). The frozen variational autoencoder decodes these into an all-atom structure and amino acid sequence. 3 Experiments We show that Prompteina’s natural-language conditioning interface controls structure generation from prompts specifying structural and functional properties (§ 3.1 ). This control extends to protein binding, where Prompteina directly steers the binder–target interface (§ 3.2.1 ) and gives agent-written designs higher interface confidence than state-of-the-art binder design models do (§ 3.2.2 ). Iterative revision yields the largest interface-confidence gains with Prompteina, especially on the hardest targets (§ 3.2.3 ). Finally, we prospectively design and experimentally test candidates against GM2A, identifying nine binders among 89 designs assayed by surface plasmon resonance (§ 3.3 ). 3.1 Text-Guided Structure Generation We first test Prompteina on prompts for structural properties (§ 3.1.1 ) or protein function (§ 3.1.2 ). Figure 3: Natural language controls global and residue-specific structural properties. Examples span global properties (shape, architecture, domain composition, and symmetry), residue-specific properties (disulfide and salt-bridge counts), and combinations of both (fold class with disulfide count). All structures match their captions and are designable (scRMSD < 2 <2 Å). Table 1: Prompteina controls the broadest range of structural properties. (a) Text-guided models. All models receive identical free-form prompts for 18 tasks in five property columns. Cells average task scores by column; parentheses give task counts (full results in Table 11 ). † denotes accuracy within 2.1 pp of chance (33.3%). (b) Property-specific models. Baselines use property-specific labels or structured inputs. Columns show tasks supported by at least one baseline; dashes mark unsupported tasks. We report within-prompt half-widths of 95% stratified-bootstrap intervals. (a) Accuracy (%) ( ↑ \uparrow ) Spearman ρ \rho ( ↑ \uparrow ) Accuracy (%) / ρ \rho ( ↑ \uparrow ) Method Fold (6) Shape (3) Secondary (3) Tertiary (2) Fold + sec./tert. (4) Prompteina 53.1 62.2 0.82 0.48 90.2 / 0.60 Chroma (text) 10.9 34.2 † 0.52 0.35 33.9 † / 0.33 Pinal 12.7 35.1 † 0.38 0.17 35.4 † / 0.12 BioMatrix 9.9 32.7 † 0.32 0.18 31.4 † / 0.15 (b) Accuracy (%) ( ↑ \uparrow ) Spearman ρ \rho ( ↑ \uparrow ) Method CATH class CATH arch. Compactness Helix Strand Sheet Prompteina 96.0 ± \pm 3.0 51.1 ± \pm 1.6 76.7 ± \pm 5.3 0.94 ± \pm 0.01 0.88 ± \pm 0.02 0.64 ± \pm 0.04 Chroma (label) 64.7 ± \pm 7.7 7.5 ± \pm 1.0 39.3 ± \pm 5.3 0.86 ± \pm 0.02 0.58 ± \pm 0.04 0.59 ± \pm 0.05 Proteina 96.7 ± \pm 3.0 27.5 ± \pm 1.4 — — — — RFdiffusion — — — 0.87 ± \pm 0.01 0.92 ± \pm 0.01 0.82 ± \pm 0.02 3.1.1 Control of Structural Properties Baselines. For structural control, we benchmark text-guided models that accept free-form prompts and property-specific models that take labels or structured inputs. Text-guided models receive the same free-form prompts as Prompteina: Chroma (text) uses a structure-captioning model for inference-time text guidance ( Ingraham et al., 2023 ) , whereas Pinal ( Dai et al., 2025 ) and BioMatrix ( Pei et al., 2026 ) generate amino acid sequences from natural-language descriptions, which we fold with ESMFold. Property-specific models, comprising Chroma (label) ( Ingraham et al., 2023 ) , Proteina ( Geffner et al., 2025 ) , and RFdiffusion ( Watson et al., 2023 ) , receive their native labels or structured inputs. For each baseline, we specify every property it supports and evaluate it only on tasks expressible through its conditioning interface. All use paper-default settings (App. E ). Evaluation. We compare Prompteina with six baselines across 18 tasks organized into five property groups: fold and topology, secondary structure, tertiary structure, global shape and surface properties, and combinations of fold class with secondary-structure or disulfide counts (Table 1 a). Complete task definitions and scoring procedures are included in App. E . For categorical properties, we report accuracy, and for count-valued properties such as helix count, we report the Spearman rank correlation ( ρ \rho ) between requested and realized values measured in each generated structure. Prompteina enables new and broader forms of structural control. Across the benchmark, Prompteina controls all five property groups and leads on 15 of 18 tasks (Table 1 a and Table 11 ). It also enables CATH labels for multiple domains in one protein and prompts specifying multiple structural constraints, such as fold class and helix or disulfide count (Table 11 ). With one natural-language interface, Prompteina nearly matches Proteina on CATH class and leads property-specific models on CATH architecture, compactness, and helix count (Table 1 b). RFdiffusion performs better on strand and sheet counts because it accepts per-residue secondary-structure inputs. Prompteina’s structural control is robust to paraphrasing (App. E.1 ) and preserves designability and novelty, with a higher designable fraction than every baseline on shared tasks and more novel designable structures than Complexa (Tables 14 and 15 ). We show representative Prompteina samples in Fig. 3 , with additional designable examples and their refolds in App. Fig. 7 . 3.1.2 Generation from Functional Specifications We next test whether Prompteina can generate structures for protein families, such as lysozymes and green fluorescent proteins, from functional prompts. In this setting, we compare against Pinal ( Dai et al., 2025 ) and BioMatrix ( Pei et al., 2026 ) , which generate sequences from functional prompts; we fold their outputs with ESMFold. Since functional prompts lack a directly verifiable structural property, we evaluate each generated protein with ProTrek ( Su et al., 2025 ) , a contrastive encoder of sequences, structures, and text. We report similarities between each prompt and its generated sequence or structure. A high ProTrek score is less meaningful for a low-confidence predicted fold, so we also weight each score by predicted-structure confidence (pLDDT). We use four prompt formats for all 122 families, including at least one from each model’s training distribution. Table 2: Prompteina leads on functional prompts. Each cell reports a model’s highest mean across four prompt formats, with a 95% bootstrap CI over 122 families. pLDDT-weighted scores multiply each ProTrek similarity by mean per-residue pLDDT divided by 100. No samples are filtered. Sequence similarity ( ↑ \uparrow ) Structure similarity ( ↑ \uparrow ) Method Unweighted pLDDT-weighted Unweighted pLDDT-weighted Prompteina 8.46 ± \pm 0.98 7.12 ± \pm 0.88 7.36 ± \pm 1.04 6.20 ± \pm 0.90 Pinal 7.55 ± \pm 0.79 5.98 ± \pm 0.70 7.09 ± \pm 0.73 5.49 ± \pm 0.68 BioMatrix 5.73 ± \pm 0.68 3.70 ± \pm 0.58 4.64 ± \pm 0.63 3.20 ± \pm 0.56 Prompteina generates structures consistent with functional specifications. At each model’s best prompt format, Prompteina achieves the highest mean on both ProTrek similarity metrics (Table 2 ). With pLDDT weighting, it significantly outperforms BioMatrix on both metrics and Pinal on sequence similarity, while retaining the highest mean ProTrek structure similarity (Table 2 ; App. F ). 3.2 Text-Guided Protein Binder Design Designing strong binders requires control over both global binder properties, such as fold class, and the size and chemistry of the binder–target interface ( Cao et al., 2022 ; Watson et al., 2023 ) . We test whether Prompteina can steer these properties through natural language (§ 3.2.1 ) and produce better predicted binders than methods using predefined, property-specific inputs (§§ 3.2.2 – 3.2.3 ). 3.2.1 Binder–Target Interface Steering We first test control over binder–target interface size, which is associated with binding specificity ( Prasad Bahadur et al., 2004 ) . We use interface residue count, defined as the number of binder residues that contact the target, as a proxy (App. G.1 ). Across 20 targets from the Complexa binder-design benchmark ( Didi et al., 2026 ) , we generate binders with Prompteina while requesting interface residue counts from 8 to 30 and holding the target and binder-length distribution fixed. For each target, we compare requested and realized counts using Spearman correlation ( ρ \rho ) and a linear fit. Prompteina reliably steers binder–target interface residue count. At finer structural scales, Prompteina steers the number of residues at the binder–target interface across 20 targets ( ρ > 0.99 \rho>0.99 , § 3.2.1 ). Beyond steering individual interface properties, we evaluate Prompteina in agent-guided protein binder design. The same language-model agent writes specifications based on the properties supported by each model’s conditioning interface. Prompteina outperforms every baseline on at least 13 of 20 targets and raises interface confidence by 14% over the strongest baseline (§ 3.2.2 ). When we allow the agent to iteratively refine designs, Prompteina shows larger gains over matched-budget i.i.d. generation than either baseline, especially on the most difficult targets (§ 3.2.3 ). As a proof of concept, we conducted a prospective, agent-guided design campaign against GM2 ganglioside activator protein (GM2A), a therapeutic target implicated in GM2 gangliosidosis ( Deschenes et al., 2023 ) . GM2A has no reported de novo binders and was one of three targets without a hit in a prior campaign ( Stark et al., 2026 ) . In our campaign, nine of 89 assayed designs were classified as binders, with the strongest yielding an overall apparent K D K_{\mathrm{D}} of 107 nM across three replicates (§ 3.3 ). These results establish natural language as an effective conditioning interface, enabling structural and functional control across scales and integrating language-based reasoning and iterative refinement into protein design. We make our code, data, and model weights available on GitHub . 2 Text-guided Protein Structure Generation A natural-language conditioning interface should let protein designers specify properties across structural scales, from global properties of the whole protein, such as fold class and overall shape, to residue-specific properties, such as disulfide bonds, catalytic sites, and binder–target contacts. We therefore construct Prompteina-Data, a dataset pairing protein structures with natural-language descriptions spanning these scales (§ 2.1 ), and use it to train Prompteina, an all-atom structure generation model conditioned on natural language for monomer and binder design (Fig. 2 ; §§ 2.2 – 2.3 ). Figure 2: Paired text–structure data and text-conditioned structure generation . (a) Structural and functional annotations are curated and (b) passed to a large language model for caption generation. (c) Residues are aligned to their corresponding caption text spans for supervised alignment fine-tuning. (d) Captions are embedded into pooled and per-token text representations, then projected to condition the structure generation model. (e) The denoiser is first trained on caption–structure pairs with a flow-matching objective, then fine-tuned with supervised text–residue alignment (§ 2.2 ). 2.1 Prompteina-Data: Text–Structure Data We construct Prompteina-Data from experimental structures in the Protein Data Bank ( Berman et al., 2000 , PDB;) , predicted structures in the AlphaFold Database ( Varadi et al., 2022 , AFDB;) , and Teddymer synthetic dimers ( Didi et al., 2026 ) (App. B.1 ). Prompteina generates one chain at a time, so we treat each chain as a separate entry, giving about 1.8M entries. The dataset includes up to 59 annotations per entry, derived from database fields and atomic coordinates (Fig. 2 a; App. B.2 ). Annotations span global properties, including fold class and compactness, and residue-specific properties with residue positions, such as disulfide bonds, catalytic sites, and protein–protein contacts. At inference, prompts may specify one property or combine several, so we vary caption content and length in the training data ( Wu et al., 2025 ) (App. B.3 ). For each entry, we sample several subsets that differ in the number and choice of annotations, then prompt Qwen3-235B-A22B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) to write one caption from each subset (Fig. 2 b; App. B.4 ). In total, we generate 52.4M captions, averaging 29 captions per entry. We use an LLM judge to compare 80 generated captions with their ground-truth annotations (App. B.5 ). Across this sample, the generated captions match their ground-truth annotations closely (97.8% recall, 89.8% precision, and 95.7% accuracy). 2.2 Prompteina: Text-Conditioned Structure Generation Our model, Prompteina, builds on the pretrained Complexa model ( Didi et al., 2026 ) (App. C.1 ), adding two text-conditioning pathways and an auxiliary text–residue alignment objective. Global and residue-level text conditioning. Complexa’s denoiser generates backbone coordinates and one side-chain latent per residue before a frozen variational autoencoder decodes both into an all-atom structure and amino acid sequence. To give every residue the same conditioning signal for global properties, we broadcast a pooled embedding from frozen Qwen3-Embedding-8B ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) through adaptive layer normalization. For residue-specific properties, each residue attends to frozen Qwen3-8B token states ( Yang et al., 2025 ) via cross-attention before protein self-attention in each denoiser layer (Fig. 2 d; Apps. C.2 – C.3 ). Two-layer MLPs map both representations to denoiser dimensions. We ablate pooled conditioning, cross-attention, and their combination, which performs best across tasks (App. D ). Text–residue alignment. In text-conditioned pretraining, we train the denoiser using a flow-matching loss but do not directly supervise which residues correspond to each text span. Prompteina-Data contains residue positions for many annotations, which we use to construct text–residue alignment annotations (Fig. 2 c). For each Prompteina-Data annotation selected for a caption, we call its associated residue positions the annotation’s residue span. A residue span contains, for example, the helix residues for a mainly alpha fold annotation and the participating residues for a disulfide bond or protein–protein contact. We attempt to locate the corresponding text span with regular expressions and TF-IDF-weighted token matching. If either span is unavailable, we retain the caption–structure pair but omit that alignment annotation. We validate span matching on held-out captions (App. B.6 ). We train an auxiliary alignment head on these annotations, following work using segmentation masks for token-level supervision in text-to-image diffusion ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . For N N protein residues and T T caption tokens, we represent alignment annotations as a binary matrix 𝐌 ∈ { 0 , 1 } N × T \mathbf{M}\in\{0,1\}^{N\times T} , where M n , i = 1 M_{n,i}=1 when token i i is aligned to residue n n . The alignment head predicts a logit A n , i A_{n,i} using cross-attention updates for every residue–token pair (App. C.4 ). Let 𝒱 ⊆ { 1 , … , N } × { 1 , … , T } \mathcal{V}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}\times\{1,\ldots,T\} contain residue–token pairs used for alignment supervision, and let σ \sigma denote the sigmoid function. Aligned residue–token pairs are sparse, so for each supervised example we set w + w_{+} to the ratio of negative to positive pairs (App. C.4 ). The alignment loss is ℒ align = − 1 | 𝒱 | ∑ ( n , i ) ∈ 𝒱 [ w + M n , i log σ ( A n , i ) + ( 1 − M n , i ) log ( 1 − σ ( A n , i ) ) ] . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{(n,i)\in\mathcal{V}}\left[w_{+}M_{n,i}\log\sigma(A_{n,i})+(1-M_{n,i})\log\!\left(1-\sigma(A_{n,i})\right)\right]. (1) After alignment fine-tuning, Prompteina gains finer control over features such as disulfide-bond and salt-bridge counts and retains global fold control without the alignment head at inference (Table 10 ). 2.3 Training and Inference Training. We first adapt the Complexa denoiser to natural-language conditioning using newly initialized parameters for pooled and token-level text conditioning (§ 2.2 ; App. C.5 ). These parameters are first trained with the denoiser frozen before we unfreeze it for joint text-conditioned continual pretraining on Prompteina-Data, following staged training in text-to-image models ( Chen et al., 2023 ) (Fig. 2 e; App. C.6 ). For alignment fine-tuning, we freeze the denoiser and update text projectors, cross-attention layers, and alignment head. We describe other Complexa training modifications that improve performance and their ablations (Apps. C.6 , D ). Inference. At inference, Prompteina takes a prompt and protein length and, for binder design, a target structure and optional target contact residues. Prompteina samples backbone coordinates and side-chain latents with the same stochastic differential equation as Complexa and uses classifier-free guidance to adjust text-conditioning strength ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) (App. C.7 ). The frozen variational autoencoder decodes these into an all-atom structure and amino acid sequence. 3 Experiments We show that Prompteina’s natural-language conditioning interface controls structure generation from prompts specifying structural and functional properties (§ 3.1 ). This control extends to protein binding, where Prompteina directly steers the binder–target interface (§ 3.2.1 ) and gives agent-written designs higher interface confidence than state-of-the-art binder design models do (§ 3.2.2 ). Iterative revision yields the largest interface-confidence gains with Prompteina, especially on the hardest targets (§ 3.2.3 ). Finally, we prospectively design and experimentally test candidates against GM2A, identifying nine binders among 89 designs assayed by surface plasmon resonance (§ 3.3 ). 3.1 Text-Guided Structure Generation We first test Prompteina on prompts for structural properties (§ 3.1.1 ) or protein function (§ 3.1.2 ). Property-specific models, comprising Chroma (label) ( Ingraham et al., 2023 ) , Proteina ( Geffner et al., 2025 ) , and RFdiffusion ( Watson et al., 2023 ) , receive their native labels or structured inputs. For each baseline, we specify every property it supports and evaluate it only on tasks expressible through its conditioning interface. All use paper-default settings (App. E ). Evaluation. We compare Prompteina with six baselines across 18 tasks organized into five property groups: fold and topology, secondary structure, tertiary structure, global shape and surface properties, and combinations of fold class with secondary-structure or disulfide counts (Table 1 a). Complete task definitions and scoring procedures are included in App. E . For categorical properties, we report accuracy, and for count-valued properties such as helix count, we report the Spearman rank correlation ( ρ \rho ) between requested and realized values measured in each generated structure. Prompteina enables new and broader forms of structural control. Across the benchmark, Prompteina controls all five property groups and leads on 15 of 18 tasks (Table 1 a and Table 11 ). It also enables CATH labels for multiple domains in one protein and prompts specifying multiple structural constraints, such as fold class and helix or disulfide count (Table 11 ). With one natural-language interface, Prompteina nearly matches Proteina on CATH class and leads property-specific models on CATH architecture, compactness, and helix count (Table 1 b). RFdiffusion performs better on strand and sheet counts because it accepts per-residue secondary-structure inputs. Prompteina’s structural control is robust to paraphrasing (App. E.1 ) and preserves designability and novelty, with a higher designable fraction than every baseline on shared tasks and more novel designable structures than Complexa (Tables 14 and 15 ). We show representative Prompteina samples in Fig. 3 , with additional designable examples and their refolds in App. Fig. 7 . 3.1.2 Generation from Functional Specifications We next test whether Prompteina can generate structures for protein families, such as lysozymes and green fluorescent proteins, from functional prompts. In this setting, we compare against Pinal ( Dai et al., 2025 ) and BioMatrix ( Pei et al., 2026 ) , which generate sequences from functional prompts; we fold their outputs with ESMFold. Since functional prompts lack a directly verifiable structural property, we evaluate each generated protein with ProTrek ( Su et al., 2025 ) , a contrastive encoder of sequences, structures, and text. We report similarities between each prompt and its generated sequence or structure. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.13909 (cs) [Submitted on 9 Oct 2026] Title: Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping Authors: Danil Rudenko , Georgii Bulgakov , Nikolay Kartashev , Ivan Rubachev , Daniil Krasylnikov , Artem Babenko View a PDF of the paper titled Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping, by Danil Rudenko and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: While deep learning models for tabular data have recently received significant research attention, the choice of objective functions for regression tasks remains an understudied degree of freedom. Several lines of research offer alternatives to the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE), but differences in datasets, backbones, and evaluation protocols make their practical benefits difficult to compare. In this work, we address this gap by performing a systematic re-evaluation of regression objectives across a broad collection of established tabular datasets and multiple neural backbones. Our comparison reveals that many proposed objectives provide limited or inconsistent gains over a properly tuned MSE baseline, while quantile loss yields consistent aggregate improvements over MSE across the tested backbones. We then identify a limitation that remains even with this strong objective: regions with different levels of target noise can reach their best predictive performance at different training epochs. Consequently, a single global early-stopping checkpoint can impose a compromise between uncertainty regions, even when the objective can represent heteroskedastic target distributions. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce a heteroskedasticity-aware extension of quantile loss that uses input-dependent label smoothing as a potential remedy and improves over quantile loss on several backbones. Overall, our results provide a modern empirical picture of regression objectives for tabular deep learning and highlight how differences in optimal stopping times across uncertainty regions can limit the effectiveness of global early stopping. The code is available at this https URL . Quantile regression under heteroskedasticity The benchmark in Section identifies several regression objectives that consistently outperform the MSE baseline. While HL-Gaussian and quantile regression (QR) perform comparably on a plain MLP, QR is more robust across backbones (Table ). Therefore, we focus on QR for the remainder of our analysis. This flexibility is particularly beneficial for tabular data, where the conditional variance Var ⁡ [ y ∣ x ] \mathrm{Var}[y\mid x] , often termed data uncertainty , changes substantially with x x (i.e., the data is heteroskedastic ). Kartashev et al. [11] identify regions of low and high data uncertainty in several established tabular datasets, and demonstrate that dataset-wise aggregate scores often obscure how methods perform across these different regions. However, modeling input-dependent distributions does not guarantee that regions with different noise levels achieve their optimal predictive performance at the same epoch. Standard global early stopping selects a single checkpoint based on average validation error, applying it uniformly to all inputs. We first examine how prediction errors evolve during training across different uncertainty levels (Section ). We then test whether selecting checkpoints separately for different uncertainty cohorts improves upon doing so for random cohorts of the same size (Section ). Together, these experiments reveal an optimization challenge that distributional flexibility alone cannot resolve, motivating the adaptive objective introduced in Section . Both experiments in this section require a per-point estimate of data uncertainty and are most interpretable when this estimate is exact and test targets are noise-free. We use two variants sharing exactly the same f f and x x : heteroskedastic , with ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ ​ ( x ) 2 ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma(x)^{2}) , and homoskedastic , with ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) , serving as a control. Importantly, for this dataset, levels of true data uncertainty σ 2 \sigma^{2} are known to us exactly. See Appendix for details. To estimate uncertainty on real data we use a CatBoost model [ 35 ] trained via Gaussian negative log-likelihood on the real datasets, utilizing the predicted σ ⁡ ( x ) \sigma(x) as our uncertainty estimate. To prevent data leakage, this estimator is fit exclusively on the training split and applied to validation and test points during inference. 4.1 Optimal stopping epochs vary by uncertainty region In this subsection we investigate whether models require different stopping epochs for regions with varying data uncertainty. This requires analyzing the test error disaggregated by uncertainty level across epochs. The uncertainty plot [ 11 ] provides this perspective. Figure (a) shows an MLP trained with the quantile loss on the heteroskedastic synthetic dataset. Each curve corresponds to one epoch and displays the point-wise change in squared error relative to a reference epoch (the one with the best aggregate validation MSE), plotted against data uncertainty. Before the reference epoch, the model performs better on high-uncertainty points and worse on low-uncertainty ones; afterward, this trend reverses. In other words, the model starts overfitting high-uncertainty regions before it finishes fitting low-uncertainty ones, and the reference epoch is merely a compromise between these competing dynamics. To verify that this pattern stems from varying noise levels rather than intrinsic properties of x x or f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) , Figure (c) repeats the experiment on the homoskedastic variant (same f f , constant noise scale, with samples sorted as in the heteroskedastic version). The effect disappears: performance changes across the displayed epochs are largely unrelated to the uncertainty ordering inherited from the heteroskedastic variant. Ideally, a model would retain its early-epoch error on high-uncertainty points while achieving its late-epoch error on low-uncertainty points, improving upon the QR baseline. However, Figure (a) only illustrates this misalignment on synthetic data and does not quantify the resulting performance loss. Section closes both gaps. This approach requires dividing the validation and test sets into groups of comparable data uncertainty, termed cohorts . To construct these, we compute the K − 1 K-1 empirical k K \tfrac{k}{K} -quantiles of the estimated uncertainty σ ^ ​ ( x ) \hat{\sigma}(x) on the validation set. These thresholds are used to split both the validation and test sets into K K cohorts, ordered from lowest (cohort 1 1 ) to highest (cohort K K ) uncertainty. Deriving these thresholds strictly from the validation set prevents data leakage, yielding equal-sized validation cohorts and test cohorts that are balanced up to sampling noise. With the cohorts established, we save a model checkpoint at every epoch during training. For each uncertainty cohort k k , we select the checkpoint e k ∗ e_{k}^{*} that minimizes the validation MSE restricted specifically to that group. During inference, each test point is routed to the checkpoint e k ∗ e_{k}^{*} corresponding to its uncertainty cohort. Because this approach assigns exactly one checkpoint to each test example, the resulting aggregated test RMSE reflects the empirical benefit of tailoring stopping times to local uncertainty levels. To accurately isolate this benefit, we cannot simply compare the resulting RMSE to standard global early stopping. While per-cohort selection allows the model to choose K K different epochs, each choice relies on only a fraction ( 1 / K 1/K ) of the validation data. To create a fair baseline, we apply the exact same procedure to random cohorts of matching size, created by randomly permuting the points before splitting. These random groups suffer the same penalty of smaller validation sets but contain no uncertainty information. Therefore, comparing uncertainty cohorts directly to random cohorts isolates the advantage of grouping by local noise levels. Table presents the relative improvements in test RMSE when using uncertainty-based (U) and random (R) cohorts compared to standard global (G) early stopping. Following the same evaluation protocol, we train TabPack with periodic feature embeddings [ 33 ] , TabM-mini with PLE-Q embeddings [ 31 ] , and RealMLP [ 34 ] . Implementation details are provided in Appendix . Table shows that quantile loss provides more consistent gains across the tested backbones than HL-Gaussian. On TabPack, HL-Gaussian has more losses than wins against MSE, despite a small positive median improvement; on RealMLP, its median gain is also limited. In contrast, quantile loss achieves positive median improvements and more wins than losses on every tested backbone. These results support quantile loss as a practical alternative to MSE, while showing that its benefits remain dataset-dependent. Quantile regression under heteroskedasticity The benchmark in Section identifies several regression objectives that consistently outperform the MSE baseline. While HL-Gaussian and quantile regression (QR) perform comparably on a plain MLP, QR is more robust across backbones (Table ). Therefore, we focus on QR for the remainder of our analysis. QR predicts conditional quantiles without assuming a parametric family for p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) , allowing the predicted distribution’s shape and scale to vary across inputs. This flexibility is particularly beneficial for tabular data, where the conditional variance Var ⁡ [ y ∣ x ] \mathrm{Var}[y\mid x] , often termed data uncertainty , changes substantially with x x (i.e., the data is heteroskedastic ). Kartashev et al. [11] identify regions of low and high data uncertainty in several established tabular datasets, and demonstrate that dataset-wise aggregate scores often obscure how methods perform across these different regions. However, modeling input-dependent distributions does not guarantee that regions with different noise levels achieve their optimal predictive performance at the same epoch. Standard global early stopping selects a single checkpoint based on average validation error, applying it uniformly to all inputs. We first examine how prediction errors evolve during training across different uncertainty levels (Section ). We then test whether selecting checkpoints separately for different uncertainty cohorts improves upon doing so for random cohorts of the same size (Section ). Together, these experiments reveal an optimization challenge that distributional flexibility alone cannot resolve, motivating the adaptive objective introduced in Section . Both experiments in this section require a per-point estimate of data uncertainty and are most interpretable when this estimate is exact and test targets are noise-free. To demonstrate the claims of this section in a controlled environment that has these traits, we construct a synthetic dataset y = f ⁡ ( x ) + ε y=f(x)+\varepsilon , with noise added only to training targets, so test RMSE directly measures recovery of f = 𝔼 ⁡ [ y ∣ x ] f=\mathbb{E}[y\mid x] . We use two variants sharing exactly the same f f and x x : heteroskedastic , with ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ ​ ( x ) 2 ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma(x)^{2}) , and homoskedastic , with ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) , serving as a control. Importantly, for this dataset, levels of true data uncertainty σ 2 \sigma^{2} are known to us exactly. See Appendix for details. To estimate uncertainty on real data we use a CatBoost model [ 35 ] trained via Gaussian negative log-likelihood on the real datasets, utilizing the predicted σ ⁡ ( x ) \sigma(x) as our uncertainty estimate. To prevent data leakage, this estimator is fit exclusively on the training split and applied to validation and test points during inference. 4.1 Optimal stopping epochs vary by uncertainty region In this subsection we investigate whether models require different stopping epochs for regions with varying data uncertainty. This requires analyzing the test error disaggregated by uncertainty level across epochs. The uncertainty plot [ 11 ] provides this perspective. Figure (a) shows an MLP trained with the quantile loss on the heteroskedastic synthetic dataset. Each curve corresponds to one epoch and displays the point-wise change in squared error relative to a reference epoch (the one with the best aggregate validation MSE), plotted against data uncertainty. Before the reference epoch, the model performs better on high-uncertainty points and worse on low-uncertainty ones; afterward, this trend reverses. In other words, the model starts overfitting high-uncertainty regions before it finishes fitting low-uncertainty ones, and the reference epoch is merely a compromise between these competing dynamics. To verify that this pattern stems from varying noise levels rather than intrinsic properties of x x or f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) , Figure (c) repeats the experiment on the homoskedastic variant (same f f , constant noise scale, with samples sorted as in the heteroskedastic version). The effect disappears: performance changes across the displayed epochs are largely unrelated to the uncertainty ordering inherited from the heteroskedastic variant. Ideally, a model would retain its early-epoch error on high-uncertainty points while achieving its late-epoch error on low-uncertainty points, improving upon the QR baseline. However, Figure (a) only illustrates this misalignment on synthetic data and does not quantify the resulting performance loss. Section closes both gaps. Figure 2: In this synthetic experiment, heteroskedastic noise creates a mismatch between the stopping epochs preferred by low- and high-uncertainty regions, while AdaQR mitigates this effect. Uncertainty plots [ 11 ] for an MLP trained with (a) quantile loss and (b) AdaQR on the heteroskedastic dataset, and (c) quantile loss on the homoskedastic counterpart. Each curve shows the smoothed point-wise difference in squared test error relative to the reference epoch with the best aggregate validation MSE; negative values indicate improvement. Test samples are ordered by increasing uncertainty in the heteroskedastic dataset, with the same ordering used in all panels. Under heteroskedastic noise, earlier epochs perform relatively better on high-uncertainty points and later epochs on low-uncertainty points, indicating that different uncertainty regions favor different stopping times. This separation is reduced with AdaQR and disappears when the noise is homoskedastic. 4.2 Measuring the impact of epoch misalignment To quantify the performance penalty implied by the epoch misalignment in Figure (a), we evaluate a hypothetical strategy of per-cohort early stopping . This approach requires dividing the validation and test sets into groups of comparable data uncertainty, termed cohorts . To construct these, we compute the K − 1 K-1 empirical k K \tfrac{k}{K} -quantiles of the estimated uncertainty σ ^ ​ ( x ) \hat{\sigma}(x) on the validation set. These thresholds are used to split both the validation and test sets into K K cohorts, ordered from lowest (cohort 1 1 ) to highest (cohort K K ) uncertainty. Deriving these thresholds strictly from the validation set prevents data leakage, yielding equal-sized validation cohorts and test cohorts that are balanced up to sampling noise. With the cohorts established, we save a model checkpoint at every epoch during training. For each uncertainty cohort k k , we select the checkpoint e k ∗ e_{k}^{*} that minimizes the validation MSE restricted specifically to that group. During inference, each test point is routed to the checkpoint e k ∗ e_{k}^{*} corresponding to its uncertainty cohort. Because this approach assigns exactly one checkpoint to each test example, the resulting aggregated test RMSE reflects the empirical benefit of tailoring stopping times to local uncertainty levels. To accurately isolate this benefit, we cannot simply compare the resulting RMSE to standard global early stopping. While per-cohort selection allows the model to choose K K different epochs, each choice relies on only a fraction ( 1 / K 1/K ) of the validation data. To create a fair baseline, we apply the exact same procedure to random cohorts of matching size, created by randomly permuting the points before splitting. These random groups suffer the same penalty of smaller validation sets but contain no uncertainty information. Therefore, comparing uncertainty cohorts directly to random cohorts isolates the advantage of grouping by local noise levels. Table presents the relative improvements in test RMSE when using uncertainty-based (U) and random (R) cohorts compared to standard global (G) early stopping. To minimize the negative effects of smaller validation sets, we restrict this experiment to the seven largest datasets from our benchmark, reporting results for K = 5 K=5 and K = 10 K=10 . The results demonstrate that uncertainty-based selection improves median RMSE over global selection by 0.18% and 0.114% for five and ten cohorts, respectively. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.13948 (cs) [Submitted on 9 Oct 2026] Title: Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game? Authors: Alexander Hickey , Joanna Knight , James Bishop View a PDF of the paper titled Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game?, by Alexander Hickey and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Language models increasingly support or automate information retrieval from document collections too large to index. This task is difficult when it requires specialist linguistic or scientific knowledge. We used the Wikipedia Game to test language models on an analogous information retrieval task. In the game, players must reach a target article using only article links. We compared sentence embedding models and LLMs across five Wikipedia languages and five academic-literature datasets. We construct very large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and of paper citations using OpenAlex and provide code to build and navigate them. This allows the study of language models' navigation capabilities without relying on third-party APIs. We compared the models with human and TF-IDF benchmarks. The Wikipedia Game format enables robust comparisons across techniques, languages, and domains. No model significantly outperformed humans, although the best models (GPT-o3 mini, GPT-4o, QwQ:32B, and DeepSeek-R1:70B) achieved comparable success. Performance and rankings varied across languages and topics, with implications for practitioners utilising these techniques. items.content: Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game? Alexander Hickey Joanna Knight James Bishop Affiliation: The Alan Turing Institute, 96 Euston Rd., London NW1 2DB, UK Email: ahickey@turing.ac.uk Abstract Language models increasingly support or automate information retrieval from document collections too large to index. This task is difficult when it requires specialist linguistic or scientific knowledge. We used the Wikipedia Game to test language models on an analogous information retrieval task. In the game, players must reach a target article using only article links. We compared sentence embedding models and LLMs across five Wikipedia languages and five academic-literature datasets. We construct very large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and of paper citations using OpenAlex and provide code to build and navigate them. This allows the study of language models’ navigation capabilities without relying on third-party APIs. We compared the models with human and TF-IDF benchmarks. The Wikipedia Game format enables robust comparisons across techniques, languages, and domains. No model significantly outperformed humans, although the best models (GPT-o3 mini, GPT-4o, QwQ:32B, and DeepSeek-R1:70B) achieved comparable success. Performance and rankings varied across languages and topics, with implications for practitioners utilising these techniques. 1 Introduction This project investigates the capabilities and limitations of language models when automatically navigating the content of unstructured document stores. Language models are often used to automate time-consuming tasks, and many of these, such as information retrieval, text classification, and question answering, require the models to connect concepts semantically [ 19 , 7 , 41 , 20 , 1 ] . We use the Wikipedia Game as an analogous task and present a comparison of human performance alongside an evaluation of the capabilities of various models across different topics and languages. This work constructed multiple vast and navigable graph datasets and the code to do so is available at: https://github.com/alan-turing-institute/ARC-Wiki-Game Wikipedia is a free online encyclopedia that contains millions of hyperlinked articles created by over a quarter of a million editors and is available in over 300 languages. In the Wikipedia Game, participants start with two random articles and are expected to navigate between them by clicking only on links within each article. Succeeding in the Wikipedia Game requires players to continuously evaluate the relatedness between the target article and the linked articles available. While sentence embedding models are naturally built to assess the similarity between segments of text, large language models (LLMs) might also possess the ability to simulate strategies, which could provide a competitive advantage [ 15 ] . Throughout this report, LLM refers to a generative prompt-based model like GPT-4o or Llama. Previous literature has discussed the Wikipedia Game, and recent natural language processing (NLP) research has started to evaluate LLMs on the game. So far, all this work has assessed the dataset via an API [ 27 ] or has used a small subset of the full graph [ 9 , 33 , 48 , 54 ] ; this is also true of demos produced by HuggingFace and TypeSafe AI. This project explores the ability of language models to play these games on Wikipedia articles in a variety of languages and on a dataset of academic works, OpenAlex 1 1 1 OpenAlex - https://openalex.org/ . By building these graphs to facilitate utilising these datasets, we can see how varieties of language models perform across languages and subject areas, generating insights relevant to real-world applications [ 6 ] . These findings can help inform individuals looking to incorporate these models into their data pipelines. 1.1 Wikipedia as a Graph English Wikipedia has over six million articles, which contain nearly 300 million links between them, making it the largest reference work in history. This encyclopedia can be conceptualised as a graph comprising connected nodes (the articles) and edges (the hyperlinks between the articles) [ 8 ] . Doing so has enabled other researchers to construct a knowledge graph [ 46 ] or identify useful missing links [ 40 ] . As Wikipedia is both human-written text and organised within a structured format, it has been harnessed for topic classification [ 17 ] , improving the performance of foundation models [ 52 ] , and providing reliable ground truth data for named entity recognition [ 3 ] . 1.2 Wikipedia as a Testing Ground This work leverages the size and structure of Wikipedia and similar datasets to provide a robust challenge for language models to utilise the semantic information they contain. Previous research has capitalised on these properties of Wikipedia to assess word embeddings and graph search algorithms and construct benchmarks [ 10 , 14 , 4 ] . Other studies have leveraged human performance in the Wikipedia game as a source of semantic information [ 49 , 50 ] . This work builds on these previous studies by assessing sentence embeddings and LLMs, making it possible to compare NLP methods and human abilities. Beyond language models, Wikipedia is an excellent training dataset for graph neural networks [ 39 , 28 ] . Additionally, these same techniques can be applied to citation networks in academic literature to more accurately assign papers to an academic topic [ 24 ] . 1.3 Generative and Embedding Models One may naively consider the Wikipedia Game to be a sequence of judging how related each potential next article is to the target article. Sentence embedding models are particularly well-suited for this task [ 5 ] as these models aim to produce a vector that numerically represents the meaning conveyed by a given sentence [ 37 ] . Embedding models can be optimised to connect related concepts or to focus on distinguishing topics or sentiments [ 2 ] , work in multiple languages [ 38 ] and address specialised domains [ 35 ] . When people play the Wikipedia Game, they do not just jump incrementally to the most related article but are instead planning a route ahead. This kind of planning and strategy cannot be reproduced by an embedding model that relies solely on a greedy iterative approach that always seeks the next ‘closest’ article. Reinforcement Learning (RL) can be used to incorporate strategic considerations into deep learning techniques, and there are numerous examples of combining RL with NLP techniques (e.g. playing text adventure games [ 34 , 31 ] ). There is some evidence that LLMs can plan and show strategic considerations [ 15 , 53 ] , which could give an advantage over embedding models. However, there are many examples where their strategic considerations fall short of what might be expected based on their language comprehension ability [ 44 , 32 ] . This issue may arise because the majority of LLM training is based on next-word prediction; it is theorised that the model’s reasoning processes quickly deteriorate once it is outside examples provided in the training data [ 29 , 51 ] . Comparing LLMs’ performance at this task to sentence embedding models, which can only provide semantic comparisons of sentences, might help illuminate their strategic ability. Figure 1: Properties of the graphs that the language models will explore. Shown here is a comparison between the five different language versions of Wikipedia and the five different topics of scientific literature included in the OpenAlex dataset. Panel A shows the overall size of the dataset with the blue bars and the number of links between articles with the red dots. Panel B shows the connectivity between the various data sets. For one thousand randomly chosen pairs of articles, the line represents what fraction is reachable within a certain number of steps. The fraction does not reach 100% because not every article is reachable from every other article. The unreachable pairs of articles were excluded from any of the experiments with the language models. 2 Datasets Most of our results are presented for English Wikipedia; however, we tested the models on a collection of different graph datasets so that the performance across languages and technical subjects can be explored. Five datasets in different languages were obtained from Wikipedia, while the subject-specific datasets were compiled from a collection of abstracts in the scientific literature. Statistics comprising these datasets can be found in Appendix C . 2.1 Wikipedia in Many Languages English Wikipedia contains over six million articles and four and a half billion words. 2 2 2 Size of Wikipedia - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Size_of_Wikipedia These articles cross-reference each other with links, which produces a navigable graph across a large fraction of the articles. We used Wikipedia in five different languages which are shown in Figure 1 A with more details in Appendix A . Four of these are considered high-resource languages (English, French, Chinese, and Russian), whereas Bengali is considered a lower-resource language [ 26 ] . A directed graph is created for each language using the Wikipedia datasets, with the nodes representing articles and the edges representing links between articles. The title and a summary containing the start of the article are stored with each node. Note that the graph is not symmetric: if Article A has a link to Article B, this does not guarantee that Article B contains a link to Article A. 2.2 OpenAlex OpenAlex is a dataset of metadata (including the title, authors, abstract, and references) about academic works. The OpenAlex data have been used to create graphs with the references and citations as the links between the articles, and the abstracts were used like the summaries. To create datasets more similar to Wikipedia, this project limited the type of work to ‘articles’ (other types of work that were excluded include ‘book chapters’, ‘dissertations’ and ‘letters’). Unlike the Wikipedia dataset, the OpenAlex datasets are symmetric graphs because if Article A references Article B, then Article B will be cited by Article A. The OpenAlex dataset was categorised based on each paper’s primary academic field to create multiple graphs (additional details in Appendix B ). Using the primary topic categorisation, five subjects were chosen (see Figure 1 A ). The connectivity of the graphs reflects the referencing patterns within each academic field, leading to significant variations in the graphs’ navigability. Figure 1 B illustrates the proportion of the graph that is reachable after a given number of steps. One article in each pair was labelled the source article and the other the target article; the pair was discarded if it was not possible to navigate between them. The goal of the game is to navigate to the target article using only the links in the graph. In the two formulations of the game, the agent player may only see the title of each link or the title and the summary text of each possible link (resembling the mouse-over preview in Wikipedia). In both formulations, the agent is allowed to see the summary of the target article. Only the choices on the ‘current’ article can be viewed before one is selected: the agent is not allowed to look further ahead or to work backwards from the target article. When the agents played the game, there were a few ways that it could end, the simplest being that the target article was reached successfully. However, the agent can fail to reach the target article in multiple ways, the most common being not reaching the target within 100 steps. It was also possible for the model to reach a dead end, for the LLM-based agents to repeatedly generate an article title that does not exist or reject the request, and for reasoning models to fail to provide an answer. The setup for all these methods is optimised to compare how these techniques might be used in a real-world setting. 4.1 Sentence Embeddings Sentence embedding models map text to numerical vectors within a high-dimensional space where semantically similar sentences are positioned closely together [ 18 ] . The ‘closest’ link was determined by the minimum cosine distance. As with all the agents, additional logic prevents them from returning to an article they have already visited to avoid becoming trapped in loops. It is possible to play the game either by comparing the summaries or the titles of the available articles. Both of these versions of the game were considered, and the results here focus on using the summary embeddings. The impact on performance when only using the titles can be found in Appendix K . AllMPNetBase is recommended by the Sentence Transformers documentation and is a comparable size to E5-Small, but is only trained on English language data [ 37 ] . MiniLM-L6 was one of the smallest models considered with only 22.7 million parameters [ 47 , 38 ] . This task is difficult when it requires specialist linguistic or scientific knowledge. We used the Wikipedia Game to test language models on an analogous information retrieval task. In the game, players must reach a target article using only article links. We compared sentence embedding models and LLMs across five Wikipedia languages and five academic-literature datasets. We construct very large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and of paper citations using OpenAlex and provide code to build and navigate them. This allows the study of language models’ navigation capabilities without relying on third-party APIs. We compared the models with human and TF-IDF benchmarks. The Wikipedia Game format enables robust comparisons across techniques, languages, and domains. No model significantly outperformed humans, although the best models (GPT-o3 mini, GPT-4o, QwQ:32B, and DeepSeek-R1:70B) achieved comparable success. Performance and rankings varied across languages and topics, with implications for practitioners utilising these techniques. 1 Introduction This project investigates the capabilities and limitations of language models when automatically navigating the content of unstructured document stores. Language models are often used to automate time-consuming tasks, and many of these, such as information retrieval, text classification, and question answering, require the models to connect concepts semantically [ 19 , 7 , 41 , 20 , 1 ] . We use the Wikipedia Game as an analogous task and present a comparison of human performance alongside an evaluation of the capabilities of various models across different topics and languages. This work constructed multiple vast and navigable graph datasets and the code to do so is available at: https://github.com/alan-turing-institute/ARC-Wiki-Game Wikipedia is a free online encyclopedia that contains millions of hyperlinked articles created by over a quarter of a million editors and is available in over 300 languages. In the Wikipedia Game, participants start with two random articles and are expected to navigate between them by clicking only on links within each article. Succeeding in the Wikipedia Game requires players to continuously evaluate the relatedness between the target article and the linked articles available. While sentence embedding models are naturally built to assess the similarity between segments of text, large language models (LLMs) might also possess the ability to simulate strategies, which could provide a competitive advantage [ 15 ] . Throughout this report, LLM refers to a generative prompt-based model like GPT-4o or Llama. Previous literature has discussed the Wikipedia Game, and recent natural language processing (NLP) research has started to evaluate LLMs on the game. So far, all this work has assessed the dataset via an API [ 27 ] or has used a small subset of the full graph [ 9 , 33 , 48 , 54 ] ; this is also true of demos produced by HuggingFace and TypeSafe AI. This project explores the ability of language models to play these games on Wikipedia articles in a variety of languages and on a dataset of academic works, OpenAlex 1 1 1 OpenAlex - https://openalex.org/ . By building these graphs to facilitate utilising these datasets, we can see how varieties of language models perform across languages and subject areas, generating insights relevant to real-world applications [ 6 ] . These findings can help inform individuals looking to incorporate these models into their data pipelines. 1.1 Wikipedia as a Graph English Wikipedia has over six million articles, which contain nearly 300 million links between them, making it the largest reference work in history. This encyclopedia can be conceptualised as a graph comprising connected nodes (the articles) and edges (the hyperlinks between the articles) [ 8 ] . Doing so has enabled other researchers to construct a knowledge graph [ 46 ] or identify useful missing links [ 40 ] . As Wikipedia is both human-written text and organised within a structured format, it has been harnessed for topic classification [ 17 ] , improving the performance of foundation models [ 52 ] , and providing reliable ground truth data for named entity recognition [ 3 ] . 1.2 Wikipedia as a Testing Ground This work leverages the size and structure of Wikipedia and similar datasets to provide a robust challenge for language models to utilise the semantic information they contain. Previous research has capitalised on these properties of Wikipedia to assess word embeddings and graph search algorithms and construct benchmarks [ 10 , 14 , 4 ] . Other studies have leveraged human performance in the Wikipedia game as a source of semantic information [ 49 , 50 ] . This work builds on these previous studies by assessing sentence embeddings and LLMs, making it possible to compare NLP methods and human abilities. Beyond language models, Wikipedia is an excellent training dataset for graph neural networks [ 39 , 28 ] . Additionally, these same techniques can be applied to citation networks in academic literature to more accurately assign papers to an academic topic [ 24 ] . 1.3 Generative and Embedding Models One may naively consider the Wikipedia Game to be a sequence of judging how related each potential next article is to the target article. Sentence embedding models are particularly well-suited for this task [ 5 ] as these models aim to produce a vector that numerically represents the meaning conveyed by a given sentence [ 37 ] . Embedding models can be optimised to connect related concepts or to focus on distinguishing topics or sentiments [ 2 ] , work in multiple languages [ 38 ] and address specialised domains [ 35 ] . When people play the Wikipedia Game, they do not just jump incrementally to the most related article but are instead planning a route ahead. This kind of planning and strategy cannot be reproduced by an embedding model that relies solely on a greedy iterative approach that always seeks the next ‘closest’ article. Reinforcement Learning (RL) can be used to incorporate strategic considerations into deep learning techniques, and there are numerous examples of combining RL with NLP techniques (e.g. playing text adventure games [ 34 , 31 ] ). There is some evidence that LLMs can plan and show strategic considerations [ 15 , 53 ] , which could give an advantage over embedding models. However, there are many examples where their strategic considerations fall short of what might be expected based on their language comprehension ability [ 44 , 32 ] . This issue may arise because the majority of LLM training is based on next-word prediction; it is theorised that the model’s reasoning processes quickly deteriorate once it is outside examples provided in the training data [ 29 , 51 ] . Comparing LLMs’ performance at this task to sentence embedding models, which can only provide semantic comparisons of sentences, might help illuminate their strategic ability. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.13889 (cs) [Submitted on 9 Oct 2026] Title: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics Authors: Weiliang Chen , Song Liao View a PDF of the paper titled RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics, by Weiliang Chen and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED (Reliability-Aware Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re-ranks candidates based on real-time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent, a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query-tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference. The code and dataset are available at this https URL .
