items.content: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics Conference: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management; November 07–11, 2026; Rome, Italy Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM ’26), November 07–11, 2026, Rome, Italy DOI: 10.1145/3799682.3839887 ISBN: 979-8-4007-2539-5/2026/11 CCS: Information systems Retrieval models and ranking CCS: Computing methodologies Artificial intelligence Weiliang Chen Affiliation: Department of Computer Science , Texas Tech University , Lubbock , Texas , USA email: weilchen@ttu.edu and Song Liao Affiliation: Department of Computer Science , Texas Tech University , Lubbock , Texas , USA email: song.liao@ttu.edu © cc Abstract. As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED ( R eliability- A ware T ool retrieval via E xecution D ynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re-ranks candidates based on real-time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent , a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query–tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Elliotes/EcoAgent . Keywords: AI agents; Tool retrieval; Contextual bandits; Contrastive learning † † cc-license: by 1. Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in natural language processing but are inherently unable to execute real-world actions ( Li et al., 2025 ; Naveed et al., 2025 ) . To overcome this limitation, recent systems integrate LLMs with external tools and APIs ( Mialon et al., 2023 ; Schick et al., 2023 ) , yielding autonomous AI agents that fulfill actionable requests, such as querying live databases or managing enterprise workflows ( Dong et al., 2024 ) . The fundamental bottleneck for these systems has shifted from text generation to accurately identifying and retrieving the correct entry from vast, growing tool repositories ( Patil et al., 2023 ) . Figure 1. Tool repository growth and reliability gap on the left, and skewed tag distribution on the right. Left panel shows tool repository growth timeline from February 2025 to January 2026, with total tools (blue line) and reliable tools (orange line). Right panel shows tag word cloud visualization. To address the tool retrieval challenge, existing research has focused on optimizing semantic relevance for Large Language Models (LLMs). Foundational works like ToolLLM ( Qin et al., 2023 ) and ToolExpNet ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) treat tool retrieval as a static ranking task. They use dense retrieval or experience networks to map queries to tool documentation based entirely on semantic relevance. While approaches such as TRFeedback ( Xu et al., 2024 ) and ToolRL ( Qian et al., 2025 ) incorporate execution feedback, they still aim to optimize how the LLM plans and invokes tools in a static environment. However, real AI agent tool ecosystems are far from static and highly unreliable. We crawl tool catalogs from LangChain ( LangChain AI, 2023 ) , CrewAI ( CrewAI, 2024 ) , LlamaIndex ( LlamaIndex, 2024 ) , and n8n ( n8n, 2024 ) to reveal the severity of this issue. As Figure 1 shows, despite rapid growth, over 50% of these tools exhibit critical flaws like broken links and missing authentication. Many tools are functionally similar, so retrieval cannot rely on semantics alone to identify which ones will execute successfully. To overcome this challenge, the system must adapt dynamically during execution. When a tool fails at runtime, the system must promptly adjust candidate ordering between requests. ToolRL cannot achieve this prompt adjustment because it uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) to update the LLM from batched trajectories and still targets the planner. Contextual bandits ( Li et al., 2010 ) effectively address this problem. They condition each decision on the current query and update from each individual execution outcome. Moreover, they observe feedback only for the selected tool and make immediate adjustments without retraining the semantic retriever. In this paper, we propose RATED ( R eliability- A ware T ool retrieval via E xecution D ynamics), a retrieval framework that dynamically adapts to runtime tool failures without human intervention. First, we introduce EcoAgent , a benchmark of 5,172 real-world agent tools and over 210,000 query–tool pairs. Second, RATED employs a dual-encoder fine-tuned with a contrastive objective for semantic matching, together with a lightweight contextual bandit that re-ranks the top- K K candidates using a prior based on metadata and execution feedback, enabling the system to avoid failing tools. Experiments show that RATED alone keeps fault selection below 3% and recovers at both failure rates. Under a 30% failure injection protocol, RATED reduces fault selection rate to 2.9%, compared with 86.2% for the ToolLLM API retriever, while adding only 0.172 ms latency per step over encode-only inference. 2. The EcoAgent Benchmark We construct EcoAgent, a benchmark comprising two complementary datasets. EcoAgent complements existing tool-use datasets with metadata reliability scores for every tool and with an evaluation protocol for injected execution failures. EcoAgent-Syn supports robust training with synthetic pairs, and EcoAgent-Real supports rigorous evaluation using real-world queries. We aggregate 5,172 real-world tool definitions from four open-source AI agent platforms, namely LangChain, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, and n8n. Metadata are normalized into a shared schema with functional descriptions, names, endpoints, and authentication fields, which supports retrieval text construction and reliability scoring. To operationalize tool quality, each tool receives an automated metadata reliability score between 0 and 1 from three weighted signals, namely name–description consistency, source credibility, and documentation quality, which Section 3.3 defines. The benchmark does not rely on manual per-tool ratings. Tools with scores of at least 0.8 are marked as reliable, identifying 2,940 tools, or 56.8% of the repository. The encoder is trained only on EcoAgent-Syn, while retrieval and dynamic experiment results are validated on the EcoAgent-Real test split, with hyperparameters selected on the validation split. We build EcoAgent-Syn with Gemma-3-1b ( Gemini Team, 2025 ) . For each tool, the model receives the tool name, functional description, and metadata as context and generates 10–20 task-oriented queries. Queries are restricted to 5–120 words, and near-duplicates with Jaccard similarity above 0.7 are removed to preserve intent diversity. Figure 2 shows the prompt template, which we also release with the dataset. To improve robustness against spurious correlations, each query is paired with hard negatives from SBERT ( Reimers and Gurevych, 2019 ) retrieval and random negatives. EcoAgent-Syn links 69,501 unique synthetic queries to 5,172 ground-truth tools, with 70,122 positive pairs and 140,244 negative pairs. For evaluation under realistic language distributions, we build EcoAgent-Real from ToolBench ( Qin et al., 2023 ) . Because the original dataset lacks ground-truth mappings to our tool repository, we implement a semi-automated labeling pipeline. GTE-Large ( Li et al., 2023 ) retrieves the top-5 candidates per query, discards pairs with cosine similarity below 0.7, and Gemma-3-1b verifies the remainder, retaining only pairs with functional match scores of at least 0.85. Human experts review a stratified sample of 200 queries and agree with the LLM verifier on 94% of cases. After filtering and deduplication, EcoAgent-Real contains 6,379 unique queries and 9,946 verified query–tool pairs. Prompt for Query Synthesis [Task] You are generating diverse user queries for an AI agent tool recommendation system. [Inputs] {tool_name} the tool name | {tool_description} its functional description | {num_queries} how many queries to write [Requirements] (1) Each query should be 5-120 words. (2) Vary the intent types: direct action requests, troubleshooting questions, how-to questions. (3) Use natural, conversational language. (4) DO NOT copy phrases verbatim from the tool description. (5) Make queries task-oriented and practical. [Output] One query per line, no numbering or bullets. A boxed prompt template with four labelled parts. The task line asks the model to generate diverse user queries for an AI agent tool recommendation system. The inputs are the tool name, the tool description, and the number of queries to write. Five numbered requirements ask for queries of 5 to 120 words, varied intent types, natural language, no verbatim copying from the tool description, and task-oriented phrasing. The output line asks for one query per line without numbering or bullets. Figure 2. Prompt template that generates the EcoAgent-Syn queries. Figure 3. RATED architecture with DRAGON retrieval, bandit re-ranking, and execution feedback. RATED architecture with DRAGON dual-encoder retrieval, bandit re-ranking, and execution feedback. 3. Methodology 3.1. Problem Setup We formulate agent tool retrieval as sequential decision making over a shared repository. Let 𝒰 = { a 1 , … , a M } \mathcal{U}=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{M}\} denote the tool pool, where M = 5,172 M{=}5{,}172 in EcoAgent. At step t t , the agent issues query q t q_{t} . The retriever returns a candidate set 𝒜 t ⊂ 𝒰 \mathcal{A}_{t}\subset\mathcal{U} with | 𝒜 t | = K |\mathcal{A}_{t}|=K , and the policy selects one tool a t ∈ 𝒜 t a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}_{t} for execution. The objective is to maximize the probability of successful execution. Unlike static retrieval with a fixed mapping f ⁡ ( q , a ) → { 0 , 1 } f(q,a)\rightarrow\{0,1\} , production agents must cope with tools that fail at runtime, where tool utility depends on semantic relevance S sem ​ ( q t , a ) S_{\text{sem}}(q_{t},a) and time-varying reliability. After execution, only the chosen tool yields binary feedback y t ∈ { 0 , 1 } y_{t}\in\{0,1\} , yielding partial feedback that we address with contextual bandits ( Abe et al., 2003 ) . Figure 3 summarizes the RATED pipeline. 3.2. Semantic Perception Module The semantic perception module implements the first stage of RATED. Given q t q_{t} , it scores all tools in 𝒰 \mathcal{U} by S sem S_{\text{sem}} and returns the top- K K candidate set 𝒜 t \mathcal{A}_{t} defined in Section 3.1 . The semantic encoder is based on DRAGON ( Lin et al., 2023 ) , fine-tuned on EcoAgent-Syn and frozen at deployment. New tools can be added by encoding their documentation with f T f_{T} without retraining the encoders. 3.2.1. DRAGON Dual-Encoder Architecture DRAGON provides separate query encoder f Q f_{Q} and tool encoder f T f_{T} , which suits settings where user queries and tool documentation follow different lexical patterns. For query q q and tool a a , we take CLS representations and L2-normalize them. The semantic relevance score is the dot product of the normalized vectors. We fine-tune f Q f_{Q} and f T f_{T} on EcoAgent-Syn with an in-batch InfoNCE objective ( van den Oord et al., 2019 ) . As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED ( R eliability- A ware T ool retrieval via E xecution D ynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re-ranks candidates based on real-time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent , a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query–tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Elliotes/EcoAgent . Keywords: AI agents; Tool retrieval; Contextual bandits; Contrastive learning † † cc-license: by 1. Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in natural language processing but are inherently unable to execute real-world actions ( Li et al., 2025 ; Naveed et al., 2025 ) . To overcome this limitation, recent systems integrate LLMs with external tools and APIs ( Mialon et al., 2023 ; Schick et al., 2023 ) , yielding autonomous AI agents that fulfill actionable requests, such as querying live databases or managing enterprise workflows ( Dong et al., 2024 ) . The fundamental bottleneck for these systems has shifted from text generation to accurately identifying and retrieving the correct entry from vast, growing tool repositories ( Patil et al., 2023 ) . Figure 1. Tool repository growth and reliability gap on the left, and skewed tag distribution on the right. Left panel shows tool repository growth timeline from February 2025 to January 2026, with total tools (blue line) and reliable tools (orange line). Right panel shows tag word cloud visualization. To address the tool retrieval challenge, existing research has focused on optimizing semantic relevance for Large Language Models (LLMs). Foundational works like ToolLLM ( Qin et al., 2023 ) and ToolExpNet ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) treat tool retrieval as a static ranking task. They use dense retrieval or experience networks to map queries to tool documentation based entirely on semantic relevance. While approaches such as TRFeedback ( Xu et al., 2024 ) and ToolRL ( Qian et al., 2025 ) incorporate execution feedback, they still aim to optimize how the LLM plans and invokes tools in a static environment. However, real AI agent tool ecosystems are far from static and highly unreliable. We crawl tool catalogs from LangChain ( LangChain AI, 2023 ) , CrewAI ( CrewAI, 2024 ) , LlamaIndex ( LlamaIndex, 2024 ) , and n8n ( n8n, 2024 ) to reveal the severity of this issue. As Figure 1 shows, despite rapid growth, over 50% of these tools exhibit critical flaws like broken links and missing authentication. Many tools are functionally similar, so retrieval cannot rely on semantics alone to identify which ones will execute successfully. To overcome this challenge, the system must adapt dynamically during execution. When a tool fails at runtime, the system must promptly adjust candidate ordering between requests. ToolRL cannot achieve this prompt adjustment because it uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) to update the LLM from batched trajectories and still targets the planner. Contextual bandits ( Li et al., 2010 ) effectively address this problem. They condition each decision on the current query and update from each individual execution outcome. Moreover, they observe feedback only for the selected tool and make immediate adjustments without retraining the semantic retriever. In this paper, we propose RATED ( R eliability- A ware T ool retrieval via E xecution D ynamics), a retrieval framework that dynamically adapts to runtime tool failures without human intervention. First, we introduce EcoAgent , a benchmark of 5,172 real-world agent tools and over 210,000 query–tool pairs. Second, RATED employs a dual-encoder fine-tuned with a contrastive objective for semantic matching, together with a lightweight contextual bandit that re-ranks the top- K K candidates using a prior based on metadata and execution feedback, enabling the system to avoid failing tools. Experiments show that RATED alone keeps fault selection below 3% and recovers at both failure rates. Under a 30% failure injection protocol, RATED reduces fault selection rate to 2.9%, compared with 86.2% for the ToolLLM API retriever, while adding only 0.172 ms latency per step over encode-only inference. 2. The EcoAgent Benchmark We construct EcoAgent, a benchmark comprising two complementary datasets. EcoAgent complements existing tool-use datasets with metadata reliability scores for every tool and with an evaluation protocol for injected execution failures. EcoAgent-Syn supports robust training with synthetic pairs, and EcoAgent-Real supports rigorous evaluation using real-world queries. We aggregate 5,172 real-world tool definitions from four open-source AI agent platforms, namely LangChain, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, and n8n. Metadata are normalized into a shared schema with functional descriptions, names, endpoints, and authentication fields, which supports retrieval text construction and reliability scoring. To operationalize tool quality, each tool receives an automated metadata reliability score between 0 and 1 from three weighted signals, namely name–description consistency, source credibility, and documentation quality, which Section 3.3 defines. The benchmark does not rely on manual per-tool ratings. Tools with scores of at least 0.8 are marked as reliable, identifying 2,940 tools, or 56.8% of the repository. The encoder is trained only on EcoAgent-Syn, while retrieval and dynamic experiment results are validated on the EcoAgent-Real test split, with hyperparameters selected on the validation split. We build EcoAgent-Syn with Gemma-3-1b ( Gemini Team, 2025 ) . For each tool, the model receives the tool name, functional description, and metadata as context and generates 10–20 task-oriented queries. Queries are restricted to 5–120 words, and near-duplicates with Jaccard similarity above 0.7 are removed to preserve intent diversity. Figure 2 shows the prompt template, which we also release with the dataset. To improve robustness against spurious correlations, each query is paired with hard negatives from SBERT ( Reimers and Gurevych, 2019 ) retrieval and random negatives. EcoAgent-Syn links 69,501 unique synthetic queries to 5,172 ground-truth tools, with 70,122 positive pairs and 140,244 negative pairs. For evaluation under realistic language distributions, we build EcoAgent-Real from ToolBench ( Qin et al., 2023 ) . Because the original dataset lacks ground-truth mappings to our tool repository, we implement a semi-automated labeling pipeline. GTE-Large ( Li et al., 2023 ) retrieves the top-5 candidates per query, discards pairs with cosine similarity below 0.7, and Gemma-3-1b verifies the remainder, retaining only pairs with functional match scores of at least 0.85. Human experts review a stratified sample of 200 queries and agree with the LLM verifier on 94% of cases. After filtering and deduplication, EcoAgent-Real contains 6,379 unique queries and 9,946 verified query–tool pairs. items.content: At a glance End-to-end forecasting: A machine learning pipeline uses forecast-time solar-wind information to generate location-specific risk estimates for 66,935 substations in the continental United States. Physics and place: The system combines Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) forecasts with local latitude, geology, and ground conductivity. Advance warning: The pipeline detected nearly 80% of major space-weather events during the evaluation period and can warn grid operators 30 to 60 minutes before a specific risk appears. Forecasting a threat to critical infrastructure During the May 2024 geomagnetic storm, utilities across North America prepared for possible impacts as auroras extended far beyond their usual range. The storm would degrade GPS accuracy and satellite operations, impacting farm operations in North America and Europe. Modern society depends on reliable electric power, yet extreme space-weather events can induce currents in transmission networks that damage equipment and increase operational risk. The challenge is not only knowing that a storm is approaching, but estimating when and where its effects could be most severe with enough warning for grid operators to respond. During my summer internship at Microsoft Research, I developed a machine learning system that forecasts space-weather risk across 66,935 substations in the continental United States. The system measures how the sun’s activity can affect the earth’s magnetic field and, ultimately, the power grid. It combines solar-wind observations, forecasts of the Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) indices, physics-informed constraints, local geological conductivity, and grid-infrastructure data to produce location-specific risk estimates 30-60 minutes ahead of potential impact. Building an end-to-end prediction pipeline Space-weather prediction is difficult because it spans several coupled systems. The solar wind changes rapidly, its interaction with Earth’s magnetosphere is irregular, and the resulting ground effects depend on local conditions. Regions with resistive bedrock can experience stronger geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) than regions with more conductive geology. Transmission-line orientation, latitude, and other power-system characteristics further influence the exposure of individual assets. Microsoft Research at BUILD 2026 Giving developers a hands-on look at some of the many AI-based models and tools they can use to accelerate innovation, enhance their capabilities, and quickly transform ideas into prototypes. Learn more Opens in a new tab The pipeline addresses this complexity in three stages, shown in Figure 1. First, solar-wind measurements from the L1 Lagrange point are used to generate forecasts of the AE and Dst indices, while geological conductivity and location features are assembled for each substation. Second, a gradient-boosting model combines these forecasted and location-specific inputs to estimate dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC risk. Finally, the resulting predictions are converted into location-specific risk estimates and aggregated into a continental risk assessment. A system of 50 AI agents helped explore features, validation strategies, and model configurations across the pipeline. Only public data sources were used, included NASA OMNI and NASA-aggregated Kyoto World Data Center data, INTERMAGNET and U.S. Geological Survey magnetometer observations, and GridSFM-derived grid data. Figure 1. End-to-end forecasting pipeline from L1 solar-wind measurements to location-specific risk estimates across 66,935 U.S. substations. Evaluating geomagnetic forecasts and infrastructure risk The AE predictor was designed to forecast rare, high-intensity geomagnetic activity that drives infrastructure risk. In the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the model produced forecasts spanning nearly the full observed range of AE activity and outperformed several empirical solar-wind-based approaches. The Dst predictor provided an additional signal describing large-scale geomagnetic storm strength. During the most geomagnetically active periods of the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the machine-learning model outperformed the Burton equation on 62.2% of individual hours. The model also produced a substantially wider prediction range than Burton-style approaches and improved severe-event detection in the end-to-end forecasting system by 1.2 percentage points when combined with AE forecasts. Predictor Result Baseline comparison Impact AE 410.2 nT RMSE Lower RMSE than empirical and solar-wind-only baselines Captures extreme-event activity used by the GIC forecasting system Dst 7.2 nT RMSE Outperformed Burton on 62.2% of peak-activity hours and provided wider prediction range +1.2pp severe storm detection when integrated into final GIC system The GIC risk stage was evaluated differently. There is no equivalent widely deployed operational system that provides a direct industry benchmark for this calculation, so the machine learning model was compared with simple linear regression. As Figure 2 shows, the system achieved detection rates of 76.5% for major events (≥10 nT/min), 81.2% for severe events (≥20 nT/min), and 64.1% for extreme events (≥50 nT/min). False-alarm rates increased with storm severity, reflecting the trade-off between missed events and cautious alerts. Performance varied by latitude, with the highest detection rates at northern stations where geomagnetic activity is strongest. Figure 2. Detection rates across storm-severity thresholds for regionally different substations, with a comparison between the average POD for each severity tier. Translating predictions into continental risk assessments The final stage translates predicted geomagnetic activity into location-specific estimates of dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC exposure. Rather than issuing a single alert for the continental United States, the system combines storm conditions with each substation’s latitude and geological factor. This produces continuous risk estimates that can distinguish lower-risk locations from areas where resistive geology can amplify ground-level effects. Figure 3 illustrates the output for a representative major-storm scenario. The map is a demonstration of the model’s continental-scale output, not a record of a live operational event. It shows how a grid operator or planner could move from a broad space-weather warning toward a more targeted view of which locations may warrant closer analysis. The current pipeline produced estimates for all 66,935 substations in approximately 333 milliseconds during measured inference, allowing many scenarios to be evaluated quickly. Figure 3. Demonstration of a continental GIC risk assessment under a representative major-storm scenario. Colors indicate modeled risk levels across 66,935 substations. Implications and looking forward This work demonstrates how physics-grounded machine learning could support more specific and timely assessment of space-weather exposure. Earlier, location-specific information could help utilities prioritize engineering review and consider targeted protective actions, such as adjusting reactive-power reserves or temporarily reconfiguring parts of the network. Further validation with utilities and operational data would be needed before the system could be used in grid operations. The project also connects with broader Microsoft Research work on AI for power systems. The open grid-data pipeline provided realistic U.S. transmission models, while GridSFM applies deep learning to AC optimal power flow for fast scenario analysis. Together, these efforts point toward richer planning and resilience workflows that combine hazard forecasts, grid topology, and power-flow analysis. Extend forecast horizons: Explore temporal-transformer approaches that capture longer-range patterns in solar-wind data and move beyond the current 30-60-minute window. Scale internationally: Adapt the system to additional regions while accounting for different geological conditions and grid topologies. Integrate with grid operations: Evaluate how forecasts could support existing decision-making and engineering-review workflows before considering higher levels of automation. Provide transformer-level risk: Add asset-specific characteristics to move from substation-level estimates toward more granular assessments of critical equipment. Related Microsoft Research work Video playback requires cookie consent GridSFM: A new, small foundation model for the electric grid Building realistic electric transmission grid dataset at scale: a pipeline from open dataset Acknowledgements Special thanks to my mentors Weiwei Yang and Spencer Fowers for their guidance throughout this project, and to Amber Hoak , Weishung Liu , and Andrea Britto for their editorial and technical feedback.
